translator: Claude (AI), draft, not reviewed by a Hittitologist
intro: The second tablet, not the last, of a ritual of Tunnawiya, the Old Woman, performed for a royal couple: the queen is mentioned in §3 and the colophon names king and queen. What survives consists of long litanies that remove sickness, curses and the 'tongues' (slander) of every kind of person from the patient's twelve body parts, rites of transfer using a ram, a sheep and a live and a dough piglet, and a mythological passage in which the Sun-god, the Mother-goddess and evil deities search the patient's body.

paras.en: […] 'white wool […]' […] they brought […] they kept black[ening …] 'those who […]'
[…] now […] and to them […] to the queen […] she keeps conj[uring …] the ariyatalli- (?) […] but heaven above […] and on them […] the titiyali- (?) […]
[…] But this one, (with?) a person(?) […] of the deep valley, this one […], this one keeps drinking water […] … is pastured(?) […] this one (is) running(?) […]

The person whom she is treating: '[…] he has not overcome the tarna- (a part of the head?) of the head, the āḫraman- (torment?) (and) the burden of the soul, the taššiyaman- (oppression?) of the bones (and) the inner parts(?); he has [no]t overcome the wa[lḫeššar-] (blow?) of the year (and) of the month,

[the markišt]awa- ḫinkan- (plague? death?) ditto (KI.MIN: the verb is to be repeated); the šarkiwali- [nakk]iwi- (?), the bloody Nergal; šātar- (?) ditto; impurity, the oa[th], [strif]e ditto; evil dreams, the fever (tapašša-) [of the body], the shortened year, the anger (of the gods), the tongue of the multitude ditto;

the tongue of the maidservant, the tongue of the bodyguard, the tongue […], [the tong]ue ditto; the tongue of the priest, the tongue of the AMA.DINGIR-LIM (a priestess, lit. 'mother of the god') ditto; the tongue [of the law]suit, of the assembly, of the auši- men (onlookers?) ditto;
[of the] lulaḫi-men (mountain folk), of the ḫapiru-men the [tong]ue, … the tongue, [di]tto; […] the fever ditto, the short[ened] (year), the anger [of the gods] and the tongue of the multitude;

[of the palace] attendant the tongue ditto, of the maidservant the tongue, [of the] bodyguard the tongue ditto, of the anointed priest the tongue ditto, [of the pries]t the tongue, of the AMA.DINGIR-LIM the tongue ditto, the tongue of the oath of the army camp ditto, [of the ḫapiru-me]n the tongue ditto, of the lulaḫi-men the tongue ditto, the tongue ditto, the tongue of the dead (and) of the living ditto, [di]tto, the tongue of the one who has eaten (and) drunk(?) ditto, the tongue of the [tangar]ant- (?) ditto, the tongue of [the šarikuwa-troops] ditto, the tongue of sorcery ditto.'

(Of) the person whom she is treating [she say]s: 'See, (either) he drove (along) a road (and) brought something (back), or to him […], or he saw something with (his) eyes, or […], or he stepped on something with (his) foot;
[…] in impurity, in sorcery, in strife […] he spoke across(?) the gods with an evil mouth;
[…] … someone […] … someone […]
[…] the day(?), the 12 limbs […] fitted together; the tarna- […], [the ear] to the ear ditto; the išḫuna- (upper arm?) [to the išḫuna-] fitted; the hand to the hands ditto; the [na]ils fitted;

[…] fitted; the limbs [fit]ted; the ḫupparatiya- (a body part) ditto; the taškuš- (a body part) to the taškuwa- ditto; the [shin(?)] to the shin(?) ditto; the foot to the foot ditto; [the pal]m to the pa[lm] ditto; the n[ails] to the nails ditto; […] to the … […]; the blood to the blood [ditto].'
For him the 12 limbs of the ram (are) [cut up(?)]; they demand(?) the sickness of the [limbs] of this man.

'Let [the head] take up(?) (the sickness of the head); the tarna- (takes up) the sickness of the tarna- ditto; … to the shoulder ditto; ditto the finger to the finger ditto; ditto the rib to the rib ditto;
[the limbs] ditto; the ḫupparti- (?) […]; [the pal]m to the palm ditto; the fingers of the hands fitted ditto; the sinew to the sinew ditto; [of the bo]ne ditto; from the blood, from the limbs,
[…] from the pig, from the ḫuntarriamma- (?) […]' [gap] […] … […] and the Old Woman […]
'[…] I pulled (it) out […] … I pulled (it) out […]'

'[From the rig]ht I pulled (it) out of him.' And she took the evil [fri]ght from him. Then she again takes up the incantation and begins to conjure; she goes around the [12] limbs in the same way. Then he comes and lies down tarrawa (in another position?), and she holds (it) over his back; she keeps conjuring exactly the same, (and) goes around the 12 limbs exactly the same.
Then he comes and lies down šark[u-…] …, and she holds a sheep over (his) chest, and the Old Woman speaks thus:
'The field, the tilled land, they plough a third time (and) a fourth time; and this person too I (treat) a third time (and) a fourth time!'
She keeps conjuring exactly the same (and) goes around the 12 limbs exactly the same.

Then they hold it (the sheep?) out to him, and he spits twice into its(?) mouth. The Old Woman speaks thus: 'Spit out the āḫra- (and) the waḫra- (both unknown)! Spit out the anger of the gods (and) the tongue of the multitude, three times, four times!'
Afterwards they bring a piglet of dough and a live piglet. They keep swinging the live pig away(?), and she keeps holding the dough piglet close to him. The Old Woman keeps speaking thus:

'The great god drove here from the town of Landa; the lai- (?) … (were) running before (him). Of illness(?), of the tongue(?) — whoever frightened (him), those who agitated him …' And she speaks the name of the one whom she is conjuring.

'We go and keep searching for him, the one walking now, the one coming(?), the eyes(?). The Sun-god became angry and sent the Ilaliyant-deities (the 'Desiring Ones'): "Where do you … (talateni, meaning unclear) him?" The one set out now(?), the coming one(?), the eyes(?) — we saw him (in the) house … (taparamma, unclear); we saw (his) eyebrow, we saw (his) eyelashes, we saw (him) with (his) 12 limbs.' And it became sweet(?) inside him(?).

'But the Mother-goddess saw him inside, and before them, the evil gods, she smeared(?) karšikarši- (?). But the evil šiwanni- (?) looked inside: "Cut them off from the eyebrows, cut them off from the eyelashes, cut them off from the 12 limbs!"' '[…] the ḫin[kan-] (plague?) of the Šarkiwali-deity, the [blood]ied Nergal ditto; she removes [fi]re (i.e. fever?) (and) šātar-;
the oa[th] ditto; sorcery, strife ditto; […]-nda ditto; evil fright ditto; evil dreams, evil birds (i.e. bad omens) ditto;

let (her) remove the shortened year; the anger of the gods, the tongue of the multitude ditto; let (her) remove the tongue of the palace attendant; the tongue of the anointed priest ditto; the tongue of the priest ditto; the tongue of the AMA.DINGIR-LIM ditto; the tongue of the troops of the army camp ditto; the tongue of the (lord of the) lawsuit ditto; the tongue of the assembly ditto; of the awišili-men (onlookers?) ditto; the tongue of the many families ditto; of the lulaḫi-men (and) of the ḫapiru-men ditto; of the dead (and) of the living ditto; the tongue of the one who has eaten (and) drunk(?) ditto; the tongue of the […]garašta- (?) ditto; let (her) remove the tongue of the [šarikuwa-troops]; the tongue of all (people) ditto.'
The person whom she is treating — she speaks his name: 'Whoever put the bronze sagari- (implements?) of Nergal on him — now … the sagari- of Nergal … I put … the god Pa[nnun]da(?) … a pig[let] …'
[Colophon:] Second tablet, not [complete]. If the king (and) the que[en …] the Old Woman […] from the earth […] to […] and him […] [rest broken]
